summary: Deprecates the use of MD5 and SHA-1 hashes in digital signatures in TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2, because those algorithms are increasingly vulnerable to attack. It does not deprecate SHA-1 when used within HMAC for record protection. The document updates RFC 5246.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9155 removes MD5 and SHA-1 from digital signatures in TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2. It does not change the use of SHA-1 with HMAC for record protection.

questions: can tls 1.2 use sha-1 for signatures
what hash algorithms are prohibited in tls 1.2 signatures
does rfc 9155 deprecate sha-1 with hmac
subtitle: Prohibits MD5 and SHA-1 for digital signatures in TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2.

tldr.problem: MD5 and SHA-1 are increasingly vulnerable to attack, yet TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 allowed them for digital signatures.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC updates TLS 1.2 rules to prohibit those hashes in digital signatures and changes the registry status of two SHA-1 signature schemes to not recommended.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9155 updates RFC 5246; it does not deprecate SHA-1 with HMAC for record protection.

today: RFC 9155 is a Proposed Standard from December 2021 and updates RFC 5246.

sections.title: Why the Signature Hashes Changed
sections.content:
TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 had specified MD5 and SHA-1 for signature hashing. The RFC describes both as vulnerable to collision attacks and cites research showing practical SHA-1 collisions.

RFC 9155 updates RFC 5246 so MD5 and SHA-1 MUST NOT be used for digital signatures. It does not deprecate SHA-1 with HMAC when used for record protection.
sections.plainLanguage: MD5 and SHA-1 can have collisions that weaken digital signatures. The update prohibits them for signatures but leaves SHA-1 with HMAC for record protection unchanged.

sections.title: Rules During the Handshake
sections.content:
Clients MUST include the signature_algorithms extension and MUST NOT include MD5 or SHA-1 in it. Servers SHOULD NOT include either hash in CertificateRequest messages.

Servers MUST NOT use MD5 or SHA-1 in ServerKeyExchange messages. If a client receives one, it MUST abort with an illegal_parameter alert. Clients also MUST NOT use them in CertificateVerify; a server receiving one must abort with that alert.
sections.plainLanguage: Neither side may use MD5 or SHA-1 for handshake signatures. A client or server that receives a prohibited signature in the specified messages must end the connection with an illegal_parameter alert.

sections.title: Registry Updates
sections.content:
IANA changed the recommended status of SHA-1-based schemes in the TLS SignatureScheme registry to N, meaning not recommended. The entries are 0x0201 (rsa_pkcs1_sha1) and 0x0203 (ecdsa_sha1); other entries remain unchanged.

IANA also updated the references for the TLS SignatureAlgorithm and TLS HashAlgorithm registries to include this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry marks two SHA-1 signature schemes as not recommended. Other entries are unchanged by this registry update.
